mappings.note: What education means to Uma -- self-belief and independent thought. Her character, C-1.1-LO-20, not the social-message LO-22.
What Gopalprasad and Ramswaroop share: both are captives of show and custom. The double-standard outcome C-1.1-LO-21.
The play's dialogue manner -- natural and satirical. C-4.3-LO-10 names samvad-shaili and vyangya.
Find passages where Ramswaroop's modern show clashes with his traditional thinking -- society's double standards, C-1.1-LO-21.
The phrase 'reedh ki haddi' used of two different characters in two senses -- the title's symbolic force, C-4.3-LO-9.
What the title symbolises -- self-respect and moral firmness. C-4.3-LO-9.
What the play satirises -- society's unjust conventions. The target of the satire is the social message, C-1.1-LO-22; C-4.3-LO-10 covers HOW the satire is worded, which this does not ask.
What 'go home and find out whether your darling son has a backbone' reveals of Shankar -- the title idiom turned on him, C-4.3-LO-9.
Imagine and write the scene if the curtain rose again -- creative composition, C-2.2.
Pick five new words, use them in sentences, guess the meanings and then check a dictionary -- vocabulary work, the language-skill competency C-4.1.

The idiom 'bheegi billi ki tarah' from the stage direction, to be explained and used in a new sentence. C-4.1 for the idiom drill -- C-4.3-LO-9 is the nearest sibling but covers only the title idiom -- and C-4.3-LO-11 because the line is a rang-nirdesh. NOTE: duplicated as the next item.
Duplicate of the previous item with its answer attached. Same mapping.
Assertion-reason: Uma did not answer the prize question because she felt humiliated -- her character, C-1.1-LO-20.
Uma likens herself to goods for sale and to sheep and goats -- her protest at the marriage custom, C-1.1-LO-22.
What Uma reveals about Shankar -- he was chased from near the girls' hostel. The revelation that exposes the family's double standard, C-1.1-LO-21.
Fill in Uma's retort: she committed no sin and showed no cowardice by peering about like his son. Her self-respect, C-1.1-LO-20.
Assertion-reason on the charge of deceit, since Ramswaroop had said Uma was only matric-pass -- the double standard, C-1.1-LO-21.
Statements about Gopalprasad: a lawyer who frequents societies yet wants a less-educated bride -- C-1.1-LO-21.
Uma's parting line about the backbone -- 'yaani backbone, backbone!'. The title idiom, C-4.3-LO-9.
Her silence turning into sobs after they leave -- Uma's character, C-1.1-LO-20.
What Ramswaroop and Ratan were doing as the play opens -- setting out the takht. Stage business and set, C-4.3-LO-11.
How Prema's appearance is given -- gandumi complexion, short. A rang-nirdesh describing a character, C-4.3-LO-11.
What Ratan is sent to fetch -- harmonium and sitar. Props that build the scene, C-4.3-LO-11.
Prema's opinion on girls' schooling -- 'aa-ee' and Stri-Subodhini are enough. The stri-shiksha message, C-1.1-LO-22.
Ramswaroop's jibe about the two gramophones -- one man-made and stoppable, the other God's. A piece of vyangya in dialogue, C-4.3-LO-10.
His instruction to dress Uma up and send her in with paan -- the bride-viewing ritual, C-1.1-LO-22.
Fill in: 'lok chaturai' dripped from Gopalprasad's eyes -- a stage direction that fixes the man and the social air, C-4.3-LO-11.
Shankar's bent waist and thin voice. The stooping back is the title metaphor made flesh (C-4.3-LO-9) and reaches us through a rang-nirdesh (C-4.3-LO-11).
Why finding the house was no trouble -- the tangewala knew the way. Plain content recall no LO here covers, so C-1.1.
Why Shankar came though college was open -- he came for the week-end. Plain recall, C-1.1.
How Gopalprasad took his tea. Plain recall, C-1.1.
His notion of taxing beauty -- the mindset that prices women, C-1.1-LO-21.
Assertion-reason: higher education is for men, women who argue wreck the home -- his orthodoxy stated outright, C-1.1-LO-21.
The ceiling he sets on a girl's schooling -- matric at most. The stri-shiksha convention the play attacks, C-1.1-LO-22.
His argument from nature -- the peacock has plumes, the peahen none. C-1.1-LO-21.
Ramswaroop laughingly adding that men have beards and women do not -- his complicity in the same orthodoxy, C-1.1-LO-21.
Fill in: the gold-rimmed spectacles seen as she raised her face -- a staging detail that springs the plot, C-4.3-LO-11.
Gopalprasad's suspicion at the spectacles -- 'not from all that studying, surely?'. Prejudice against girls' education, C-1.1-LO-22.
Which song Uma was made to sing -- part of the display demanded of a girl on view, C-1.1-LO-22.
Why she broke off mid-song -- her eyes met Shankar's. Uma's character, C-1.1-LO-20.
Which qualities her courage in facing Gopalprasad reveals -- C-1.1-LO-20.
What satire the 'tax on beauty' idea carries. The question is about the satirical turn itself, so C-4.3-LO-10, whereas the plain recall of the same line is mapped to C-1.1-LO-21.
Is Uma's weeping weakness or sensitivity, with reasons: LO-20 for her character, C-2.1 for the argued judgement the item demands.
What Ramswaroop's repeated 'han-han-han' says about him -- a character's speech habit marking his social self, C-4.3-LO-10.
Prove from the characters that the play lashes orthodox thinking on girls' education -- the social-message outcome C-1.1-LO-22.
A full account of Uma's character -- C-1.1-LO-20.
How the play exposes the flaws of arranged-marriage custom -- C-1.1-LO-22. NOTE: duplicated as the next item.
Duplicate of the previous item, with its answer attached. Same mapping: C-1.1-LO-22.
When the play was written and the state of girls' education then: LO-19 for placing the ekanki and its author, LO-22 for the stri-shiksha question.
Ramswaroop's 'baap ser hai to ladka sava ser' about Shankar -- a saying whose irony the play turns against him, C-4.3-LO-10.
Where 'reedh ki haddi' first occurs -- Gopalprasad telling Shankar to sit up straight. The title idiom's first sounding, C-4.3-LO-9.
The right account of Ramswaroop -- he affects modernity, hid Uma's degree and laughed along with the orthodoxy. C-1.1-LO-21.
The most accurate reading of Uma's character -- educated, self-respecting, brave. C-1.1-LO-20.
Why Prema wished they had stopped at Entrance -- so the girl would stay in hand and spare them trouble. The convention against educating girls, C-1.1-LO-22.
Jagdishchandra Mathur's administrative posts -- the author-introduction half of C-1.1-LO-19.
What Uma revealed about Shankar that shamed Gopalprasad -- the double standard laid bare, C-1.1-LO-21.
Why the play ends on Ratan's word 'makkhan' and what that does -- the closing irony of the dialogue, C-4.3-LO-10.
The argument he built on the peacock and the lion -- C-1.1-LO-21.
Mathur's best-known staged play -- author introduction, C-1.1-LO-19.
What Uma meant by the furniture-shop comparison -- a girl treated as merchandise; the marriage-custom message, C-1.1-LO-22.
The pull between modernity and orthodoxy in Ramswaroop -- C-1.1-LO-21.
The main features of Gopalprasad's personality -- C-1.1-LO-21.
How Prema stands for the Indian housewife of that time -- her views on girls' schooling are the point, C-1.1-LO-22.
The significance of the moment Uma stops singing -- her character, C-1.1-LO-20.
The two senses in which 'reedh ki haddi' is used -- C-4.3-LO-9.
Why he still wanted the match though he called their views backward, and what that shows -- his double standard, C-1.1-LO-21. NOTE: duplicated as the next item.
Duplicate of the previous item, with its answer and stray options bleeding in. Same mapping: C-1.1-LO-21.
Why Shankar's studies were delayed -- a year's illness. Plain recall, C-1.1.
Which item never reached the tray -- the butter. Plain recall, C-1.1; item 56 asks what that word DOES at the close and is mapped to C-4.3-LO-10.
The exchange about the janampatri -- the horoscope-matching custom the play holds up, C-1.1-LO-22.
When and where Mathur was born -- author introduction, C-1.1-LO-19.
The preparations Ramswaroop makes for Uma before the boy's party arrives -- the bride-viewing custom, C-1.1-LO-22.
What Prema thinks of girls' education, with an example -- C-1.1-LO-22.
What Gopalprasad demands in a bride and how much schooling he allows -- his orthodoxy, C-1.1-LO-21.
How Shankar's body language and person are drawn: through the stage directions (C-4.3-LO-11), and what they are drawn to mean is the missing backbone (C-4.3-LO-9).
Why father and son start when Uma brings in the paan -- the spectacles betray her education, C-1.1-LO-22.
Why Ramswaroop lied about Uma's schooling -- the double standard, C-1.1-LO-21.
Compare the two men for likeness and difference -- both live by the same double standard, C-1.1-LO-21.
The part played by satire and humour, with examples -- C-4.3-LO-10.
